To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The oscillatory movements of nuclei and cells in glioma cells are driven by the cytoskeleton and its associated molecular motors; (2) The cytoskeleton of glioma cells is highly dynamic, and the forces responsible for cell and nuclear movements are not transmitted directly to the centrosome; (3) The oscillatory nuclear movements of glioma cells are similar to the meiosis specific nuclear oscillations of the fission yeast S. pombe
the actomyosine system and microturbules are involved in nuclear/cellular movements in C6 rat and human glioma cells, respectively.

the oscillatory movements of glioma cells are driven by the actomyosine contractile apparatus and microtubuli and the cell-line dependent differences in their contributions can be explained by the intrinsic tension differences of the cytoskeletal components.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying nuclear movements in mammalian cells and the results may have implications in cancer cell biology.
the role and the contribution of the various components of the cytoskeleton in nuclear migration.
the role of the cytoskeleton in cell migration and the mechanical properties of cells and tissues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nuclear oscillations are a highly dynamic and cell-type specific process, which involves a variety of mechanical components.
the nuclear movements of glioma cells are highly complex and cell-line specific, which makes them an interesting model for studying the mechanical properties of the cytoskeleton.
both the actin and the microtubule cytoskeleton are involved in nuclear movements in both cell types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nuclear movements are driven by a complex network of cytoskeletal elements.
the nuclear migration in C6 glioma cells can be explained by the interplay between dynein, microtubule and microtubular associated proteins.
we could show that nuclear movements can be studied in a cell line dependent manner, and that we have found a new mechanism of nuclear oscillations in glioma cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cytoskeletal elements of mammalian cells are highly integrated and the mechanical forces they generate are tightly coupled.
nuclear movements are not only driven by the cytoskeleton but that the mechanical environment of the nucleus is also important for the regulation of nuclear migration.
nuclear migration in glioma cells involves the actomyosins system and the microtubule network in a cell-line dependent manner.
